evidence: The code at src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:106-113 relies on token.token_type is TokenType.TABLE (tokenizing via resolved.tokenize(sql)), and pyproject.toml:46 pins sqlglot>=30.22,<31. The claim concerns sqlglot's own tokenizer keyword tables (sqlglot/tokens.py and the postgres, mysql and sqlite dialect tokenizers) across that version range. No sqlglot source is in the head or base view, and my searches for sqlglot/tokens.py under the repo and system paths found nothing (one search timed out). I did not run sqlglot or compare any 30.x releases. The tokenizer behavior is therefore unverified. Missing evidence: sqlglot 30.22 and the latest 30.x tokens.py and dialect KEYWORDS maps, or a run of Dialect.tokenize('TABLE t') and tokenize('"table"') for each dialect.

The call site (src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:93-104) catches ValueError from sqlglot.Dialect.get_or_raise and uses resolved.tokenize(sql) with token.token_type/.text. The claim concerns sqlglot 30.31.0's dialect.py, which is not in the head view; a Glob for sqlglot/dialects/dialect.py and a Grep for 'def get_or_raise|def tokenize' in the review directory found nothing. I did not run the installed package or read it from outside the views, so the 'only ValueError' and tokenize return-shape properties cannot be confirmed.

readonly.py:105-112 compares previous = token.text.upper() against _TABLE_KEYWORD_NOT_SHORTHAND_AFTER (lines 49-70). The sqlglot source (sqlglot/tokens.py) is not in the head view or anywhere I could Glob, so I could not read what Token.text holds for DOT and keyword tokens, or whether the tokenizer merges multi-word keywords. From the listed set alone, forms such as CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE, CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE or CREATE TRANSIENT TABLE would put REPLACE, EXTERNAL or TRANSIENT directly before TABLE, and none of those is listed. The function would then report them as shorthand. The docstring (lines 85-88) says the function errs toward True, so that outcome may be intended. I did not run the tokenizer, so I could not confirm any of this. Missing evidence: the sqlglot tokens.py source, or a run of Dialect.tokenize on those statements.

readonly.py:101-113 matches each docstring assertion (81-91). Any token with token_type TokenType.TABLE returns True unless the previous token's uppercased text is in _TABLE_KEYWORD_NOT_SHORTHAND_AFTER (lines 107-110). A quoted identifier tokenizes as IDENTIFIER, not TABLE, so it never counts. Only sqlglot.errors.TokenError is caught (103-104). Any other tokenizer exception propagates. The ValueError catch at 94-100 covers only dialect lookup. Traced the hint input `SELECT a FROM t ORDER BY a DESC; TABLE users`: the token before TABLE is `;`, not DESC, so it returns True and the exemption does not hide it. A hostile `t.table` or `CREATE TABLE` is exempt as documented. Comments are not tokens, so `CREATE /*c*/ TABLE` is also exempt, which fits 'directly after a token'. I found no input where the code departs from the docstring.

The docstring at src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:73-92 says the tokenizer-based detection (TokenType.TABLE check, lines 106-112) must hold on every version, and pyproject.toml:46 bounds sqlglot to >=30.22,<31. The code is consistent with the claim as written, since it uses the tokenizer and not the parse tree. Whether the tokenizer types an unquoted TABLE as TokenType.TABLE on every release from 30.22 to 31, and whether the parse changes at 30.30, depends on sqlglot's own source. No sqlglot package is present in the head view or on the runner (Glob found no sqlglot tokens.py), and I ran no multi-version test. Missing evidence: sqlglot tokens.py for the releases across the range, or a version-matrix test run.

Grep over the head view finds exactly two production callers of uses_table_shorthand: rls.py:228 (apply_rls) and whole_row.py:124 (_whole_row_reference). apply_rls: after the check, sqlglot.parse at rls.py:234-237 catches ParseError/TokenError and raises RlsError, so a TokenError-rejected input is refused (same dialect, same raw sql, so the tokenizer fails identically). _whole_row_reference: whole_row.py:121 calls _parse_statements BEFORE uses_table_shorthand; _parse_statements (readonly.py:642-657) raises UnsafeSqlError on ParseError/TokenError and on empty SQL or unresolved dialect, and also for MySQL-ambiguous input (_mysql_parse_sql). The only preprocessing difference (readonly.py:629-635) replaces carriage returns inside comments with spaces, which does not change tokenization of the non-comment text, so no input tokenizes-fails in the helper yet parses successfully. Other uses are tests only. The claim in the docstring at readonly.py:89-91 holds. For the absolute wording, the input I traced was an unterminated string (TABLE users WHERE x = 'unterminated). It gives False from the helper and is then refused by both parse paths.

whole_row.py:121 calls _parse_statements(sql, dialect) before uses_table_shorthand (line 124). readonly.py:642-657 returns a list and converts sqlglot ParseError/TokenError (plus empty SQL and unresolvable dialect) to UnsafeSqlError, so unparseable SQL raises 'could not parse SQL' before the TABLE check can return 'TABLE'. Absolute-style input: a TABLE s.t that sqlglot rejects raises at line 121 and never reaches line 124.

whole_row.py:121-125 _whole_row_reference calls _parse_statements first; readonly.py:652-657 converts ParseError/TokenError into UnsafeSqlError('could not parse SQL'), so a TABLE s.t that does not parse is refused as unparseable. If it does parse (30.31 as SELECT * FROM s.t), the docstring wording 'that does not parse' does not claim otherwise, and line 124 returns 'TABLE' (whole-row refusal) via uses_table_shorthand. uses_table_shorthand (readonly.py:101-113) tokenizes the whole SQL and flags any TABLE token not after '.' or a command keyword, so TABLE t in any statement or subquery (after ;, (, WITH, set operators) is refused. Hostile input considered: `SELECT 1 WHERE x IN (TABLE t)` yields TABLE after '(' so True. Docstring matches the code.

rls.py:228-232 apply_rls calls uses_table_shorthand(sql, dialect) before sqlglot.parse (line 235) and raises RlsError('row-level security can only scope SELECT-shaped reads; refusing ' 'a TABLE statement'), which concatenates to contain 'refusing a TABLE statement'. tests/unit/test_safety_rls.py:371 and :385 match that text; line 358 matches 'could not prove', present at rls.py:334. RlsGuardRunner (safety/__init__.py:197-203) wraps the message verbatim in a new RlsError via f-string with no message-dependent branching, so the substring is preserved for callers.

readonly.py imports only stdlib/sqlglot (lines 15-24), no sqllens modules, so it cannot import rls. rls.py:44 imports it; rls imports sqllens.config (line 43), whose only safety imports are function-local lazy imports of safety.masking (config.py:306,315). safety/__init__.py imports readonly (line 58) before rls (line 67), so package init order is safe. whole_row already imports readonly (line 78) the same way. uses_table_shorthand is defined at readonly.py:73, no leading underscore, and readonly.py has no __all__, so it is public and importable.

tests/unit/test_safety_table_shorthand.py:47-66 (the cited lines 371-384 are past EOF; the file has 78 lines, but the excerpted cases are at lines 52-57) parametrize test_other_sql_is_not_flagged over DIALECTS = postgres, mysql, sqlite, None and assert not uses_table_shorthand. Implementation src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:93-113 tokenizes with the dialect and returns True only for an unquoted TokenType.TABLE token whose previous token text is not in _TABLE_KEYWORD_NOT_SHORTHAND_AFTER (contains '.', 'CREATE', and so on). Traced: a comment (`-- TABLE users`, with a space after `--` so MySQL also treats it as a comment) produces no token. A string literal ('TABLE users'), and "table" in MySQL, is a STRING token. A quoted identifier in the other dialects is an IDENTIFIER token. `t.table` has previous token '.', which is excluded. `SHOW CREATE TABLE users` either has TABLE preceded by CREATE, or SHOW is a command and the rest becomes one string token. All paths return False in every listed dialect. I did not run the tests or read the sqlglot source, so the tokenizer behavior comes from my knowledge of sqlglot and the code above.

The assertion is at tests/unit/test_safety_table_shorthand.py:71 (source_line 392 is stale; the file has 78 lines). uses_table_shorthand (src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:101-104) calls resolved.tokenize(sql) and returns False on sqlglot.errors.TokenError, before it scans for TABLE tokens. sqlglot's tokenizer raises TokenError ('Missing \' from ...') on an unterminated string literal instead of returning partial tokens. I read this from knowledge of sqlglot, not by running it. The repo's existing test test_untokenizable_sql_is_empty (tests/unit/test_safety_limits.py:279) and the readonly.py:128 docstring rely on the same behavior (unterminated string gives TokenError). So the test's expectation of False through the TokenError path matches the code. I did not run sqlglot.

The cited line 395 does not exist (the head test file has 78 lines), so I located the test by symbol. It is test_unknown_dialect_warns_and_uses_no_dialect at tests/unit/test_safety_table_shorthand.py:74-77. It runs caplog.at_level(WARNING, logger="sqllens.safety.readonly"), asserts uses_table_shorthand("TABLE users", "no-such-dialect") is truthy, and asserts "unknown sqlglot dialect" is in caplog.text. In src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py, line 26 sets logger = logging.getLogger("sqllens.safety.readonly"). Lines 93-100 catch ValueError from sqlglot.Dialect.get_or_raise(dialect), call logger.warning("uses_table_shorthand: unknown sqlglot dialect %r; ..."), then fall back to the no-dialect tokenizer. That fallback tokenizes "TABLE users" to a TABLE token with no preceding keyword, so the shorthand is detected. The logger name and message text match what the test uses. The ValueError catch matches the exception type sqlglot's get_or_raise raises for an unknown dialect; I did not read sqlglot itself to confirm this. Caveat: the test does not check the record's logger name. at_level only sets that logger's level, and caplog.text covers all captured records. The logger name is therefore exercised only indirectly.

pyproject.toml:46 declares "sqlglot>=30.22,<31"; requirements.txt:104 locks sqlglot==30.31.0, which is inside that range. A repo-wide case-insensitive grep for sqlglot specifiers/versions (outside docs) found only these two pins plus prose; docker/requirements-drivers.txt (the only other requirements file) has no sqlglot entry, and no Dockerfile/workflow/other constraint file pins sqlglot. Remaining 30.2x/30.30 mentions are comments/docs about behavior, not constraints; the floor 30.22 is the lowest anywhere.

apply_rls (rls.py:228) and assert_no_whole_row_select (whole_row.py:124) both call uses_table_shorthand before parsing. It tokenizes (readonly.py:93-113) and returns True for any TABLE keyword token unless the preceding token is in _TABLE_KEYWORD_NOT_SHORTHAND_AFTER (., CREATE, DROP, CHECK, etc.), so it does not depend on sqlglot's parse shape and applies on every version. I tried the hint's counterexamples. A preceding excluded token needs a command keyword or a dot directly before TABLE, and those forms are not TABLE t queries. A TokenError gives False, but then sqlglot.parse in rls.py:234-237 raises TokenError, which is wrapped as RlsError, so it still fails closed. The comment at rls.py:224-227 and the docs describe the same behaviour (pre-30.30 parsed to a shape the scope walk missed, 30.30+ parsed to a SELECT). I did not run RLS against sqlglot 30.30+ to confirm the prior rewrite, so that historical claim rests on those authored comments.

readonly.py:73-113: uses_table_shorthand tokenizes with the dialect and returns True for every token of type TokenType.TABLE unless the previous token's uppercased text is in _TABLE_KEYWORD_NOT_SHORTHAND_AFTER (lines 49-70: '.', CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, LOCK, RENAME, DESCRIBE, DESC, TEMPORARY, TEMP, UNLOGGED, VIRTUAL, ANALYZE, CHECK, CHECKSUM, OPTIMIZE, REPAIR). The doc (read-only-safety.md:225) says 'such as CREATE, DROP or MySQL's CHECK', so the list is given as examples and the claim matches. A quoted "table" is tokenized as an identifier (VAR/IDENTIFIER), not TokenType.TABLE, so it is never flagged; the docstring says the same (lines 81-82). Absolute-claim input traced: 'SELECT 1; TABLE t', '(TABLE t)', 'UNION TABLE t' and 'WITH x AS (...) TABLE t' all have a previous token of ';', '(', UNION or ')', none in the set, so each is flagged. A previous token whose text only equals a listed word, such as a string literal 'drop', cannot start a TABLE t query, since the shorthand needs a separator, '(' or a set operator before it. I found no input that evades the guard. I did not run the tokenizer on each dialect, and the quoted-identifier point rests on reading the code.

rls.py:228 calls uses_table_shorthand(sql, dialect) and raises RlsError before sqlglot.parse at rls.py:235. readonly.py:73-113 tokenizes with the dialect and returns True for any TokenType.TABLE token anywhere (any statement or subquery) unless the previous token text is in the exempt set (., CREATE, DROP, ALTER, DESC, CHECK etc.). It does not depend on the parse tree, so it behaves the same on every sqlglot version. Counterexample tried for the absolute claim: a TokenError, which makes the function return False (readonly.py:103-104). The parse at rls.py:235 tokenizes the same SQL and raises TokenError, which becomes RlsError (rls.py:236-237), so it still fails closed. Exempt predecessors were also tried. A TABLE query can only start after a statement start, ';', '(', a set operator or a CTE close. None of those texts is in the exempt set, and the exempt-keyword forms (CREATE TABLE, DESC TABLE and so on) are non-Query statements that rls.py:252 refuses anyway. I found no input where a TABLE query slips through.

tests/unit/test_safety_rls.py:374-386 parametrizes dialect over postgres/sqlite/mysql and asserts RlsError matching 'refusing a TABLE statement' for both statements. apply_rls (src/sqllens/safety/rls.py:228-232) first calls uses_table_shorthand and raises RlsError('...refusing a TABLE statement'). uses_table_shorthand (readonly.py:93-113) flags any TokenType.TABLE token unless the previous token text is in the exclusion set (readonly.py:49-69), which contains neither UNION nor ')' nor the CTE name 'x' / AS. The prior defect (a fixed predecessor allowlist at SEMICOLON/L_PAREN/set operators) is fixed at head. readonly.py:106-112 flags every TokenType.TABLE token unless the previous token's uppercased text is in _TABLE_KEYWORD_NOT_SHORTHAND_AFTER (49-70: '.', CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, LOCK, RENAME, DESCRIBE, DESC, TEMPORARY, TEMP, UNLOGGED, VIRTUAL, ANALYZE, CHECK, CHECKSUM, OPTIMIZE, REPAIR). The docstring (81-85) says exactly this, so it matches the loop. The prior probes now behave as follows. 'WITH x AS (SELECT 1) TABLE users' follows R_PAREN, so it is flagged. 'CREATE TABLE a AS TABLE t' flags the second TABLE (previous is AS). 'INSERT INTO a TABLE t' is flagged. 'EXPLAIN TABLE t' is flagged (previous is EXPLAIN). The only accepted TABLE t position behind an exempt token is EXPLAIN ANALYZE TABLE t. The exemption is described in the docstring, not omitted. The callers rls.py:228 and whole_row.py:124 then parse, and EXPLAIN is not an allowed SELECT-shaped root (readonly.py:331-335 allow-list of Select, Union and With). I did not trace the Command fallback to the end.

The defect was fixed. At head, uses_table_shorthand (src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:73-113) no longer requires TABLE to start the statement or follow ;, (, set operators. It returns True for every TokenType.TABLE token unless the previous token is in _TABLE_KEYWORD_NOT_SHORTHAND_AFTER (., CREATE, DROP, etc.; lines 49-70). In `WITH x AS (SELECT 1 AS id) TABLE orders` the previous token is `)`, which is not in the set, so it returns True. It is detected from the tokenizer, so the result does not depend on the sqlglot version. I read the code but did not run it under sqlglot 30.29.0 and 30.31.0. The dependent claims now match the code: the docstring (readonly.py:81-91), the comment in rls.py:224-227 and its refusal at 228-232, row-level-security.md:30, read-only-safety.md:225 (which lists `WITH x AS (…) TABLE t` and describes the any-TABLE-token rule) and changelog.d/373.security.md:1.

The finding still holds at head. readonly.py:40-42 `_READ_SHAPED_KEYWORDS` = {SELECT, WITH, UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT, SHOW}, with no TABLE. `first_sql_keyword` (readonly.py:116-156) returns 'TABLE' for `TABLE t`, because the token is TokenType.TABLE and KEYWORDS maps 'TABLE' to that type, so `is_read_shaped` is False. The postgres runner (postgres/sql_runner.py:173-199) and the mysql and sqlite runners (sqlite/sql_runner.py:215-222) then take the rows_affected branch instead of the capped row fetch. Those are the two guards that the finding's scenario (whole-row guard off, no RLS rules) disables. assert_select_only has no TABLE refusal (grep of readonly.py shows TABLE only in the shorthand helper and SHOW CREATE TABLE). So `TABLE t` passes the read-only guard and is misrouted. Tests: test_safety_table_shorthand.py covers only the detector, and no test combines the two guards off with a runner. Search for readers of the keyword set: is_read_shaped is called in the 3 runners and in run_sql.py:77. No criterion or No-defect reason applies, because the result is wrong output (a row count instead of rows) on a reachable configuration. Reach is limited to Postgres and MySQL with both guards disabled.
